prompt: You keep a prefix-sum array so a range total is the prefix through its right end minus the prefix before its left end. Requests alternate between range sums and frequent single-element updates. Why is this a poor choice?

options.text: Range-sum queries on a prefix array are O(n)
options.explanation: Queries are the prefix array's strength: two lookups and a subtraction, O(1).

options.text: Prefix sums only work for sorted arrays
options.explanation: Prefix sums work on any array; order is irrelevant.

options.text: Each update to `a[i]` changes every `P[j]` whose prefix includes that position, so updates are O(n)
options.explanation: Correct. Each early-position update can require rewriting most stored prefixes. A segment tree makes both operations O(log n) for n array elements.

options.text: The prefix array uses O(n²) memory

workedExample: A prefix total includes every earlier array element. Changing an early element changes all later stored prefixes, so one update can rewrite O(n) entries for n elements. A range sum is still cheap, but many updates make that layout unsuitable. A segment tree changes only the summaries on one root-to-leaf path, balancing update and query costs.

prompt:
Using the sum segment tree below (built over `a = [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7, 4]`), which stored nodes does `query(2, 5)` add together?

```
              [0,7]=39
         /              \
    [0,3]=16          [4,7]=23
    /      \          /      \
 [0,1]=7 [2,3]=9  [4,5]=12 [6,7]=11
```

options.explanation: Those nodes cover indices 0–7, far more than 2–5. A query only uses nodes lying entirely inside the range.
Correct. Indices 2–5 are exactly the union of nodes `[2,3]` (9) and `[4,5]` (12), both fully covered, so the recursion stops at those two summaries.
The sum is right, but the tree never descends to those leaves: it stops at the covered nodes `[2,3]` and `[4,5]`. Visiting leaves would make queries O(n).
Segment trees do not subtract; that would need an invertible operation and fails for min or max.

workedExample:
Trace `_q` from the root:
1. `[0,7]`: partial overlap with [2,5]. Recurse.
2. `[0,3]`: partial. Its children: `[0,1]` is disjoint (return 0); `[2,3]` is covered (return 9).
3. `[4,7]`: partial. Its children: `[4,5]` covered (return 12); `[6,7]` disjoint (return 0).
4. Combine the two covered summaries to obtain 21. The query needs neither a leaf-by-leaf scan nor subtraction.
